_note: How FeedForward uses each term. 'external' cites the body that defines it; 'methodology' terms describe this app and point to its documentation. Written by the FeedForward team; status 'draft' until reviewed by a dietitian.

terms.short: How much of a nutrient most healthy people need each day.
terms.long: FeedForward uses the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) or, where there is not enough data for one, the Adequate Intake (AI) set by the US National Academies (IOM), cross-checked against the EFSA Dietary Reference Values. The value depends on age, sex, pregnancy and breastfeeding, which is why the profile setting changes the percentages.

terms.short: A typical amount of a food eaten at once, used for every comparison.
terms.long: Comparing 100 g of every food would make dried herbs or baking powder look like superfoods. FeedForward compares one realistic portion instead: 30 g of nuts, 150 g of cooked lentils, 100 g of fish, 2 g of dried herbs. Portions are set per food group, informed by the FDA reference amounts and common EU portion guidance.

terms.short: How much of one day's need a single portion provides.
terms.long: Amount in one portion divided by your daily need. 30% means about a third of the day's need from one portion. The dots summarise it: one dot below 15%, two dots from 15%, three dots from 30%.

terms.short: A statement about a nutrient's effect that the EU has officially approved.
terms.long: Under Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, a health claim may be used only if the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) assessed the science and the European Commission authorised the exact wording, for example 'Iron contributes to normal cognitive function'. FeedForward shows these words unchanged and marks them. Anything else is labelled as a research association.

source.label: EU Register of nutrition and health claims

terms.short: A claimed effect EFSA looked at and found the evidence did not support.
terms.long: EFSA rejected many popular associations, for example that vitamin E supports heart function or that magnesium improves resistance to mental stress. FeedForward does not use these to recommend foods, and lists them in the dictionary so you can see what is not proven.

source.label: EU Register of nutrition and health claims

terms.short: A link supported by studies, but not an official EU health claim.
terms.long: Some goals, such as sleep, have no authorised EU claim for any nutrient. Where the research literature supports a link (graded A to D), FeedForward may use it, but it is never worded as a health claim and the evidence grade is shown in the science view.

terms.short: How strong the science behind a nutrient–goal link is.
terms.long: A: authorised EU claim or meta-analyses of trials. B: individual randomised trials. C: observational or mechanistic studies. D: preliminary. Stronger grades count more in the ranking.

source.label: Adapted from Oxford CEBM levels and GRADE

terms.short: How much of a nutrient your body can actually absorb from a food.
terms.long: Not everything in a food is absorbed. Iron from meat and fish (heme iron) is absorbed at around 25%, iron from plants (non-heme) at around 10%. Oxalates in spinach bind calcium so little of it is absorbed. FeedForward adjusts for these effects.

source.label: Hurrell & Egli, Am J Clin Nutr 2010 (PMID 20200263)

terms.short: A food to eat together with another to absorb more of a nutrient.
terms.long: Vitamin C raises the absorption of iron from plant foods; this is an authorised EU claim ('Vitamin C increases iron absorption'). So beans or lentils come with a tip to add peppers, citrus or kiwi. Vitamin C is not an iron source itself, so it is shown as a tip, not as a reason to pick a food for iron.

terms.short: The most of a nutrient you can have daily without risk of harm.
terms.long: The Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL). For some nutrients it applies to food (for example vitamin A from liver, iodine from seaweed); for others, such as magnesium, only to supplements. A portion above a UL is flagged and ranked lower.

terms.short: Nutrients to keep below a daily amount.
terms.long: FeedForward counts sodium against 2,300 mg, saturated fat against 22 g and sugars against 50 g a day. Foods that use a large share of these in one portion rank lower, and more so for goals they work against (salt and blood pressure).

terms.short: Foods most people know and can buy are shown before unusual ones.
terms.long: Rankings are ordered so that common foods come first; unusual items such as game meats are moved down but not hidden. This changes only the order, never what a food provides. It will be based on European consumption data once the EU food tables are added.
